source.title: On the landscape of one-hidden-layer sparse networks and beyond
source.authors: Dachao Lin; Ruoyu Sun; Zhi-Hua Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports gradient-descent training outcomes for sparse networks, including CIFAR-10, but measures squared loss rather than the claim versions’ training classification error or their specified landscape and training conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports experimental training-loss outcomes and convergence behavior for sparse networks. Its CIFAR-10 experiment uses 400 training samples with one-hot targets and MSE, so it does not report classification error. Loss values visible only in plots are recorded as figure only. Theorems about spurious valleys are theoretical arguments, not experimental training results.
record.test_reason: The study tests sparse-network loss landscapes and MSE convergence, but none of the six specified versions. Its networks are fully connected rather than convolutional; its sparse-sparse example is not a ReLU teacher-student width comparison. The initialization observation does not test activation-matched signal propagation or trainable depth.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. More precisely, benign-landscape guarantees require particular sparse structures for linear networks and stated width, data, and activation assumptions for nonlinear networks. The deep nonlinear guarantee excludes spurious valleys with nonempty interiors, rather than all spurious valleys. Sparsity in both weight layers can create spurious valleys and minima; the experiments illustrate low-MSE sparse-dense training and difficult sparse-sparse optimization.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse networks with gradient descent and squared loss; the claim versions specify other architectures, error measures, and training comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: For the CIFAR10 tanh experiment, the authors report very slow convergence with default initialization and scale weights by 10. For ReLU sparse networks they report a long stuck period and oscillation; sparse training trajectories are described as much longer and coupled with optimization methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Tested five-layer sparse nonlinear networks reach near-zero MSE; ReLU exhibits an initial plateau and late oscillation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wide sparse networks with a dense final layer can fit these regression targets, while sparsity and activation affect optimization trajectories.

fits_no_version.finding: Default initialization converges very slowly on the CIFAR-10 subset; the reported runs instead multiply initialized weights by 10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale may affect convergence in this five-layer sparse tanh setting; the paper provides a qualitative observation rather than a controlled speed estimate.

fits_no_version.finding: Hidden-output ranks vary with activation, sparsity, layer, and training progress.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse-network hidden representations can become numerically rank deficient during training despite low final MSE.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient descent encounters suboptimal outcomes in a constructed sparse-sparse example; ReLU reaches approximate global minima in 5 of 100 trials.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: One-hidden-layer networks with sparsity in both weight layers can have spurious valleys and difficult optimization.

record.problems: Experiments use 400 training samples and MSE regression, not classification error; CIFAR10 results use a sampled subset with one-hot targets. Many loss values are only in figures. The sparse-sparse table’s flattened formatting obscures its typographic groupings.

untested.parts: Convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR-10/100, random or corrupted labels, and model-size or regularization comparisons.
ReLU teacher-student optimization with a perfect solution, jointly increasing widths, and one or two extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity shortcuts, special initialization for very deep plain tanh networks, and Fixup.
Activation-matched initialization preserving signals and gradients, associated speed and depth effects, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and deep orthogonal convolutions.
Learning rates relative to the stability threshold, transient loss growth and curvature reduction, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and normalization-free Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: T6 applies relative to these claim versions, despite the study's original optimization results. States are cannot_determine relative to the specified versions, not denials of the reported MSE or landscape findings. The record's proposed sparse-sparse claim incorrectly says two hidden layers; the constructed experiment has one hidden layer and two weight layers.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, corrupted or random labels, and the stated dense-network size, optimizer, and benchmark conditions are not measured.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student width comparison.
No plain-versus-identity-shortcut depth comparison, batch-normalized ImageNet/CIFAR-10 training-error comparison, or tested special initialization for plain deep tanh networks.
No comparison of activation-matched initializations, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, or 10,000-layer convolutional training.
No learning-rate stability-limit or sharpness experiment.
No batch-normalization speed or learning-rate-tolerance comparison, or Fixup comparison.

rows.subject: 5-layer nonlinear sparse network (Tanh; CIFAR10)
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on one-hot targets with MSE; all layers except final layer pruned; weights multiplied by 10 after initialization.

conditions.value: CIFAR10, sampled subdataset of 400 training samples
total sparsity shown in Figure 4(c); individual values figure only

rows.note: Authors state all sparse structures could obtain near-zero training loss. The paper does not report classification error, and the individual plotted loss values are not stated in text.
rows.check: Near-zero MSE is explicitly reported, but this sparse fully connected CIFAR-10 subset experiment does not measure V1's convolutional-network training classification error.

rows.subject: 5-layer nonlinear sparse network (ReLU; synthetic dataset)
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on synthetic regression data with MSE; sparse structures varied.

conditions.value: total sparsity shown in Figure 4(b); individual values figure only

rows.note: The text says ReLU has near-zero loss even with large sparsity, but also describes a long stuck period at the origin and oscillation near the end.
rows.check: Synthetic regression MSE fits no version. The authors report near-zero final loss; a plateau and oscillation do not establish an incomplete final effect.

rows.subject: 5-layer nonlinear sparse network (Tanh; CIFAR10)
rows.operation_detail: Authors report that default initialization converged very slowly, then scaled each weight by 10 after initialization for the CIFAR10 run.

conditions.value: CIFAR10, sampled subdataset of 400 training samples
default PyTorch initialization; scaled weights by 10 for CIFAR10

rows.measure: Convergence speed and training MSE loss
rows.value: scaled initialization: near-zero training loss; speed value not stated
rows.note: The text reports the default initialization as very slow and says weights were scaled by 10 for CIFAR10; it does not quantify the speed difference.
rows.check: The authors report slow default initialization and then scale weights by 10. They do not report a controlled speed comparison, activation-matched signal or gradient preservation, or a depth comparison. Near-zero loss duplicates R1.

rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on synthetic regression data with MSE.
rows.measure: Rank of hidden-layer output matrices during training
rows.value: Dense network preserves full rank in first few layers but becomes rank deficient in later hidden layers.
rows.note: This is a rank result, not training classification error or one of the versions’ named outcomes.
rows.check: Hidden-output rank does not measure any version's training outcome or comparison.
